title: Wavy Walls and Roofs May Soften Hurricane Wind Forces
summary:
Engineers in Florida are testing a simple idea for storm-prone homes: give walls and roofs gentle waves, like ocean ripples, instead of flat surfaces.

Hurricane winds and related flooding cost U.S. households about $34 billion a year, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Extra bracing and rounded corners can help, but they can be expensive. Researchers at Florida A&M University and Florida State University published wind-tunnel results in the journal Engineering Structures.

They 3D-printed low-rise building models—some flat, some with wave depths of 5 percent, 7.5 percent, and 10 percent of the building's height. For a 20-foot-tall building, a 10 percent wave would stick out about 2 feet. In the tunnel, every wavy model faced lower wind loads than the flat one. The deepest waves cut peak pressure near roof and wall corners by about 40 to 60 percent. Those corners are where damaging forces often gather.

Why? Wind rushing over a flat roof can form one big swirling vortex that creates strong suction and can help peel a roof off. Over waves, the air skips like a stone on water, making many smaller swirls instead of one powerful one, so extreme suction spots are weaker.

"These nonconventional building shapes reduce the damage from worst-case severe weather scenarios," said co-author Pedro Fernández-Cabán, a Florida State University civil engineer. "It's another tool for engineers and designers to protect against wind damage."

The team cautions the study measured surface pressure on models. They are running more tests and computer models to refine wave shapes. If results hold, wavy designs could become a practical option for communities facing stronger storms.
why_it_matters: Strong storms threaten homes where families live. Clever shapes could be another affordable way engineers protect roofs and walls.

Engineers use wind tunnels to blow air over scale models and measure pressure.
A large swirling vortex over a flat roof can create strong upward suction.
Changing a building's outer shape is one way designers try to lower those peak forces.
